transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-13
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE); Jordan Blake (Crowfoot VP Eng); Priya Nair (Crowfoot Lead ML); Evan Cho (Crowfoot Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
Crowfoot looking to move away from an expensive OpenAI-heavy stack, they run a mix of hosted OpenAI calls for non-latency tasks and an internal vLLM/TGI deployment for low-latency chat. Interested in understanding Redwood hosted cost vs dedicated pools and private VPC for compliance. Security team wants KMS/HSM story and audit logs. SE asked about batch sizes, KV cache usage, and quantization.

Topics covered: current stack, latency & cost targets, deployment modes, compliance controls, benchmark plan.

Transcript: 
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everybody, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Diego, our solutions eng. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Jordan (Crowfoot): Good, thanks.
[00:08] Priya (Crowfoot): Morning all.
[00:10] Evan (Crowfoot): Hi. Sorry for being a minute late.
[00:12] Maya: No worries. Quick agenda: run through your current setup, what you're trying to achieve, constraints, then Diego will dig into compatibility and benchmarks, and we'll finish with next steps. Sound OK?
[00:22] Jordan: Yep, perfect. We're trying to figure out if we should consolidate more of our inference onto Redwood versus keep the split between OpenAI for non-sensitive generation and our vLLM/TGI instances for our latency-sensitive chat.
[00:34] Priya: To add, we're also evaluating dedicated hardware so we can get predictable p99 latency for certain customers, plus we have data residency needs for some lines of business.
[00:43] Diego (Redwood): Got it. Do you mind walking me through the numbers? Request per second, typical sequence lengths, token distribution?
[00:50] Priya: Sure. For chat, peak QPS per region is about 14 rps, typical messages about 80–120 tokens, but we have spikes to 200 tokens on long prompts. For embeddings and long-form summarization we do OpenAI calls, roughly 200–300 qps.
[01:10] Jordan: Cost is creeping up on the OpenAI side — we also want better observability so we can tie tokens to specific customers.
[01:18] Maya: That's helpful. On Redwood hosted we provide token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards, with rollups to customer IDs so you can see spend by product. Dedicated gives you isolation and predictable throughput, private gives VPC with your KMS.
[01:34] Evan: Security questions up front — do you support customer-managed KMS or HSM? Audit logs and retention controls?
[01:40] Diego: Yes, in Private mode we integrate with customer KMS and can support HSM-backed keys; we also provide audit logs and long-term retention as an add-on. For Hosted we offer encrypted-at-rest and separation, but keys are managed by Redwood unless you pick private.
[01:58] Priya: For the vLLM/TGI side, we run TGI-compatible endpoints in our datacenter behind a load balancer, and that handles low-latency chat. We're worried about parity when moving to Redwood — generation quality, stop sequences, tokenization differences.
[02:18] Diego: Totally. Our migration playbook includes a parity benchmark with your prompt set; we run identical prompts against your vLLM/TGI baseline and Redwood-hosted model variants. We measure perplexity-ish metrics, but more importantly, e2e latency, token counts, and failure modes.
[02:36] Jordan: How do you handle KV cache or prefix caching? That's been a big cost saver for us in vLLM.
[02:43] Diego: We support KV cache and prefix/KV caching patterns; we expose controls for TTL, shard sizing, and cache-hit metrics. Depending on whether you go hosted or dedicated, we can tune cache locality to minimize cross-node hops. In Dedicated you can get more predictable cache warm behavior.
[03:01] Priya: Nice. What about batching? We can't have too much batching otherwise tail latency suffers.
[03:06] Diego: We use continuous batching with latency SLOs — you set a soft latency SLO and we auto-balance batching to maximize throughput without violating p95/p99 targets. For e.g., if your p99 SLA is 150ms, we keep batching windows tiny and lean on model variants that serve faster.
[03:22] Jordan: And model variants? We sometimes run quantized models in-house. Can Redwood run int8 or int4 quantized variants?
[03:30] Diego: Yes, we have quantization profiles as part of Redwood Optimize recommendations; we can recommend int8 for most workloads, and int4 on dedicated pools where acceptable. We also label models by verified performance so you know tradeoffs.
[03:44] Evan: From compliance, we need SOC 2 evidence and penetration test reports. Also SSO (SAML/Okta) and RBAC for ops teams.
[03:52] Maya: We can share our SOC 2 type 2, pen test summaries, and our SAML SSO integration docs. RBAC and audit logging are supported on all paid tiers; private gives you more controls over retention.
[04:06] Priya: Great. On the parity side, do you support the same tokenizer as TGI/vLLM? We've hit tokenization mismatches before.
[04:14] Diego: We strive to match tokenizers of the model family; when that's tricky we include tokenization diff reports in the parity benchmark so you can see token count differences and adjust prompt engineering.
[04:25] Jordan: Ok. What about costs — can you give ballpark numbers for hosted vs dedicated? We need a delta to present to finance.
[04:33] Maya: I'll send a hosted vs dedicated pricing sheet after this call. Quick summary: hosted is pay-as-you-go per token and ideal for getting started with minimal ops; dedicated is a monthly committed capacity with lower per-token cost and guaranteed throughput; private adds platform licensing and infra costs. I'll include an example TCO for your current QPS and token patterns.
[04:54] Priya: One red flag: we have some customers in EU with residency requirements. Can Dedicated be regionally pinned?
[05:01] Diego: Yes, Dedicated pools can be region pinned; Private can be deployed in a customer VPC in a given region or on-prem depending on the package.
[05:10] Jordan: In terms of rollout strategy, we want a canary then A/B. How do rollouts work on Redwood?
[05:16] Diego: We offer canary rollouts, weighted traffic splits, and automatic fallbacks to a lower-cost model if errors spike. Also route policies so you can route by customer or latency tier.
[05:28] Evan: A few technical checks — do you expose model internals for debugging (like attention cache stats)? Our engineers rely on runtime metrics to debug hallucinations.
[05:36] Diego: We expose tracing hooks and token-level logs (configurable), KV cache stats, and per-request metadata. For hosted, we redact sensitive fields unless you're on a private deployment.
[05:47] Priya: For benchmarking, we want to run our prompts against both Redwood hosted and our vLLM baseline. Will Redwood run the hosted side or do we port models to a dedicated playground?
[05:57] Diego: Either. For parity checks we can run hosted against your baseline; if you want exact hardware parity we can spin a dedicated evaluation pool with the model variant you prefer. We'll provide a benchmark template that collects latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput, token counts, and qualitative pass/fail on top N prompt set.
[06:20] Jordan: Timing — if we want to decide in the next 30–45 days, can you support a quick pilot?
[06:25] Maya: Yes — we typically do a 2–4 week pilot: send prompts, run benchmarks, a small dedicated pool if needed, and then results + transition plan.
[06:33] Evan: Any gotchas with data retention for logs? We have a 7-year retention requirement for certain artifacts.
[06:39] Maya: Seven years is long — we have long-term retention add-ons and can export audit logs to your S3 or SIEM. That's usually part of the Private/Enterprise contract.
[06:50] Priya: One more — how mature is your TGI compatibility? We use some custom endpoints that expect TGI behavior.
[06:58] Diego: Our engineering has done several TGI/vLLM compatibility projects; we have a compatibility checklist and a shim layer for specific endpoint behaviors. We'll share the checklist and a short example of running TGI scripts.
[07:12] Jordan: Good. Ok let's run through concrete next steps.
[07:15] Maya: Recap: 1) I will send pricing and hosting comparison (hosted vs dedicated vs private) with example TCO for your traffic. 2) Diego will send the vLLM/TGI compatibility checklist and benchmark template. 3) You (Jordan/Priya) will share prompt set and SLOs. 4) We'll schedule a parity benchmark kickoff. Anything to add?
[07:34] Evan: Please include SOC2 docs and SSO integration guide in the packet.
[07:38] Maya: Will include.
[07:40] Priya: If possible, can we get an estimate for quantized model throughput on dedicated GPUs? Even rough numbers help.
[07:47] Diego: Yes we'll include int8/int4 throughput estimates and observed latencies in the checklist.
[07:53] Jordan: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[07:55] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by Friday with the docs.
[07:58] (end)

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-heard acronyms (TGI was at times transcribed as 'T G I' or 'T G E'), some punctuation dropped, speaker overlap briefly at 05:00–05:10.
